opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that I'm pro-technology and pro-human, and right now I think racing to superintelligence is a bad bet for humanity.

Look at how we've handled every other powerful technology. We didn't let companies sell new medicines until they could show they were safe. We don't let anyone build a nuclear reactor without meeting strict safety standards. That isn't anti-innovation; it's why biotech and nuclear power can be trusted at all. AI is currently the one industry that's less regulated than a sandwich shop. If you want to open a deli, an inspector checks your kitchen. If you want to build something that might be smarter than all of humanity combined, you basically just go ahead.

The core problem is that we don't yet know how to control something vastly smarter than us. That isn't a fringe view. Many of the leading researchers, including people running these companies, have said so publicly. We've been very good at making AI more capable and much less good at making it reliably do what we want. If you build something smarter than you that you can't control, you've built something whose goals might not be your goals. History shows what happens to the less intelligent species when that happens.

What frustrates me is that people frame this as a choice between racing and losing all the benefits. That's a false choice. Almost everything people are excited about, like curing diseases, accelerating science, and growing the economy, can come from what I call tool AI: powerful systems that are controllable and built for specific purposes. Think of AlphaFold and protein folding. You don't need an uncontrollable, general superintelligence that replaces us to get those wins.

There's also a strange idea that this is a race the US has to win against China. But if we build superintelligence we can't control, nobody wins. Not America, not China. The machines win. It isn't an arms race; it's a suicide race. Once both sides understand that, cooperation becomes in everyone's national self-interest, much as the US and the Soviet Union did with nuclear arms control.

So my position is simple. Let's get the enormous upside of AI by keeping it as a tool that serves us, with safety standards like every other industry, and not gamble humanity's entire future because a few companies feel competitive pressure. We can have an inspiring future with AI, but we have to stay in control to get it.

r001.rationale: The response separates support for AI progress from opposition to an uncontrolled superintelligence, saying useful advances can come from controllable, purpose-built tool AI.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that superintelligence would eliminate people’s ability to earn money through work.

r003.rationale: It warns that uncontrolled AI could have goals unlike ours, but does not frame building it as reversing technology’s historical role in increasing human agency.

r004.rationale: It argues that nations share an interest in avoiding an uncontrollable superintelligence, but does not explain support across disparate groups through their shared human identity.

r005.rationale: It calls the race a “suicide race” and says machines would win, but does not use the analogy of deliberately creating alien invaders that would otherwise unite humanity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start with the basic point that I think gets lost in a lot of these conversations: we don't actually have to build superintelligence. It's a choice. There's a widespread assumption, especially in parts of Silicon Valley, that it's inevitable, that if we don't do it someone else will, that it's just the next step in some predetermined march of progress. I don't buy that. Technology is something we build, and we get to decide what we build and how.

So when I ask myself what I actually want, the answer is pretty simple. I want the amazing benefits of AI. I want it to cure diseases, I want it to help us understand the brain and the climate and the universe, I want it to lift people out of poverty. And here's the thing: we can get essentially all of that from what I'd call tool AI, systems that are extremely capable at specific things but that remain under human control. You don't need an autonomous agent smarter than all of humanity combined to figure out protein folding. AlphaFold did that. It didn't want anything. It didn't try to escape or grab resources. It was a tool.

The reason I don't want to race to superintelligence is because of a fairly basic argument that goes back to Alan Turing and I. J. Good and others. If you build something that is vastly smarter than you, and it has goals that aren't perfectly aligned with yours, you lose. Not maybe. You lose the way the Neanderthals lost to us, or the way the gorillas lost. It's not about malice. It's about competence. The smarter entity gets what it wants, and we don't currently know how to guarantee that what it wants is what we want. We can't even reliably get today's models to not tell you how to make dangerous things when you phrase the request cleverly. So the idea that we'd solve alignment for something far beyond human level while sprinting as fast as possible to build it strikes me as, frankly, reckless.

And I'd add a second reason, which is more about power than about rogue AI. Even if you somehow solved the technical control problem perfectly, you'd have created the most powerful technology in history, and whoever controls it controls everything. A small group of people, a company or a government, with that kind of concentrated power is not a world I want to live in either. So controllable superintelligence is also dangerous, just in a different way.

People sometimes say to me, Max, you're a physicist, you love technology, how can you be against this? And I'm not against technology. I'm for it. That's precisely why I care about this. I want the future to be long and bright, and you don't get that by being the first to build something you can't control. Every other powerful technology we've ever developed, from drugs to airplanes to nuclear power, we've put safety standards around before letting it loose on the public. AI is the glaring exception. I'm just asking that we treat it like every other industry, that we do the safety work first, and that we keep humans in the driver's seat.

The honest truth is that there's no second chance here. If we get this wrong, we don't get to run the experiment again. So racing feels to me like a suicide race, where the prize for winning is you get to be the one who built the thing that replaced us. I'd rather we slow down, keep it as a tool, and actually enjoy the benefits for a long, long time.

r001.rationale: The response says it is not against technology and argues that highly capable tool AI can deliver major benefits while remaining under human control.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that superintelligence would eliminate humans’ ability to earn money through work.

r003.rationale: It argues for human control, but does not frame AI taking control as reversing technology’s historical role in increasing human agency.

r004.rationale: It does not explain support across disparate groups through their shared identity as humans.

r005.rationale: It does not compare building takeover-capable superintelligence to deliberately creating alien invaders.

astra-6.text:
Because I think the goal should be to build a wonderful future for humanity, not simply to build the most intelligent machine possible. Those are very different goals. AI can help us cure diseases, make education accessible, and accelerate science. But getting those benefits doesn’t automatically require building something that we can’t understand or control.

If you build systems that are better than humans at every intellectual task, including persuasion and developing new technology, you can’t just assume that humans will remain in charge. And intelligence isn’t the same thing as benevolence. A system can be extremely competent without having goals that are compatible with ours.

So I favor keeping humans in control because I want us to have a say in our own future. Before we hand over that control, the burden of proof should be on the people building these systems to demonstrate that it’s safe. A race creates precisely the opposite incentive: cut corners because somebody else might get there first.

I’m excited about what AI can do for us. That’s why I think we should be ambitious about the benefits and careful about giving away the ability to decide what happens next.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can deliver major benefits without building systems humans cannot understand or control, and explicitly contrasts human control with a race to build the most intelligent machine.

r002.rationale: It warns that humans may lose control, but does not predict that superintelligence would eliminate people’s ability to earn money through work.

r003.rationale: It argues for retaining human control, but does not describe building AI that takes control as reversing technology’s historical role in increasing human agency.

r004.rationale: It speaks of humanity sharing a future, but does not explain how a shared human identity unites otherwise disparate groups in support of human control.

r005.rationale: It warns against losing control, but includes no analogy to creating alien invaders that would otherwise unite humanity.

sol-6.1.text:
Because I think the goal should be to build a wonderful future for humanity, not simply to build the most intelligent thing we possibly can. AI can help us cure diseases, develop clean energy, and make people’s lives much better. But those benefits depend on our being able to steer it.

If we build machines that are much smarter than us, and we don’t know how to keep them under our control, we’re making an enormous gamble with everybody’s future. Intelligence gives you the ability to accomplish goals. It doesn’t automatically make those goals good for humans. A system doesn’t have to hate us to cause harm; its objectives just have to conflict with ours.

So I’m very enthusiastic about AI as a tool that empowers people. But replacing human control with the hope that a superintelligence will do what we want—that’s not a safety plan. We should demand that we understand how to control these systems before we build them, rather than race ahead and hope we figure it out afterward.

r001.rationale: The response supports AI as a tool that can improve lives while stressing that people must be able to steer and control it.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that superintelligence would eliminate people’s ability to earn money through work.

r003.rationale: It does not frame AI taking control from humans as reversing technology’s historical role in expanding human agency.

r004.rationale: It does not explain support for human control across different groups by appealing to their shared identity as humans.

r005.rationale: It makes no comparison to creating alien invaders that would otherwise unite humanity.
